new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable by default (moraic trochee built right-to-left), but a heavy word-final syllable (closed syllable or one containing a vowel+glide sequence: CVC, VC, VG, CVG, CVGC) takes final stress. Prefixes are never stressed; suffixation moves stress to the new penult unless the final syllable is heavy; the final vowel of long-form possessive suffixes and the clitics =ia 'LOC', =di 'PL' and suffix -uti are extrametrical.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed in prose beyond 'clash removal' and 'line conflation is not [operative]', but transcriptions consistently mark a secondary stress two syllables before the primary, e.g. [ˌku.ne.ˈnɛp] 'gecko', [ˌnu.mɑ.ˈmɑm] 'our house', [nɑ.ˌɣu.jɑ.ˈŋɑ.no.ɑ] 'his/her narrative' (alternating trochaic rhythm leftward).
new_statements.exceptions: Heavy final syllables attract final stress; prefixes never stressed; possessive-suffix final vowel extrametrical ([nu.ˈmɑ.mɑ] 'your house' but [ˌnu.mɑ.ˈmɑm] 'our house'); clitics =ia, =di and suffix -uti extrametrical ([ˈnu.mi.ɑ] 'at the house', [ˈnu.mɑ.di] 'houses') except when -uti creates a diphthong/heavy syllable ([ru.ˈhɑu.ti]).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on citation forms of monomorphemic nouns/verbs and affixed words; analysis based on the Tabares dialect. The 2005 OPD (Data Papers 47, p. 29) gives the same rule in two sentences: 'Stress is predictable and usually falls on the penultimate syllable. Exceptions occur when heavy syllables attract word-final stress.'
new_statements.identity_note: Stober's 2013 analysis is explicitly based on the Tabares dialect of Mato (the other dialect, Ramuk, differs only in the realisation of /x/; 'the grammatical systems of the dialects do not vary', p. 7). Same language as Glottolog mato1252 / ISO met; alternate names Nenaya, Nengaya, Nineia. Note Glottolog lists the grammar sketch without a volume number; the title page says Data Papers on Papua New Guinea Languages Volume 59 (not 60).
